DARS-NIC-656775-N0V8C.summary: The University of Bristol is using identifiable National Disease Registration Service (NDRS) cancer registration data, linked to men aged 50 to 69 in a prostate cancer screening trial. It is studying whether a single PSA blood test screen reduces deaths from prostate cancer and from all causes, and what screening would cost. The aim is to give evidence for UK screening policy. Results from the 10-year follow-up were published in a medical journal in 2018 and used to update patient and GP information sheets.

DARS-NIC-656777-B0V8N.summary: The University of Leeds, an academic organisation, holds national cancer registration, hospital, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy data linked to survey responses from men with prostate cancer. The data was used to understand factors linked to quality of life after diagnosis, and is now kept securely while the university plans a request to re-use it. Reported results include 15 peer-reviewed articles, reports sent to every clinical team across the UK, and a Movember web tool.

DARS-NIC-656778-L3D2T.summary: The Institute of Cancer Research is using identifiable NHS England cancer registration, hospital care and systemic anti-cancer therapy data for participants in the TACT2 breast cancer trial. It is testing whether routinely collected health data can reliably identify cancer recurrence. The intended benefit is that future breast cancer trials could use this data for long-term follow-up, reducing the burden on hospitals and participants. A poster has been presented at a Cancer Research UK conference.

DARS-NIC-656779-D9Y3Z.summary: The Institute of Cancer Research is using identifiable NHS England cancer registration, hospital (A&E, admitted patient and outpatient) and systemic anti-cancer therapy data for people who took part in the POETIC breast cancer trial. It is testing whether routine health data can reliably show when breast cancer has returned, so it could replace hospital-based follow-up in future trials. The intended benefit is less long-term follow-up burden for patients and hospitals.

DARS-NIC-656780-B1W0Y.summary: The Institute of Cancer Research is using identifiable NHS England cancer registration, hospital (A&E, admitted patient and outpatient) and systemic anti-cancer therapy data for participants in the IMPORT HIGH breast cancer trial. It is testing whether routine health data can reliably identify cancer recurrence, so it could replace hospital-based follow-up in future trials. The main intended benefit is less burden on patients and hospital staff in long-term follow-up.

DARS-NIC-656781-W4B0L.summary: The Institute of Cancer Research is using identifiable NHS England cancer registration, hospital and systemic anti-cancer therapy records for women who took part in the FAST-Forward breast radiotherapy trial. It is testing whether routinely collected health data can reliably identify breast cancer recurrence, so long-term trial follow-up need not depend on hospital-collected data. The intended benefit is less follow-up burden on hospitals and future trial participants.

DARS-NIC-656784-C7P5B.summary: The Healthcare Quality Improvement Partnership (HQIP) uses linked cancer registration, treatment, hospital and patient experience data for the National Audit of Breast Cancer in Older Patients. The audit looks at the care and outcomes of women over 70 with breast cancer in England and Wales, compared with women aged 50 to 70. It aims to give NHS providers comparative information to improve care. So far it has delivered national audit reports and quality improvement tools, and 12 published papers.

DARS-NIC-656793-T4H6S.summary: The University of Bristol is using NHS England cancer, hospital inpatient and outpatient, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and diagnostic imaging data for the ProtecT trial. The trial compares surgery, radiotherapy and active monitoring for men with low- or intermediate-risk localised prostate cancer, and the data are used to follow their outcomes over about 20 years. It aims to give patients and clinicians evidence for treatment decisions. Results from earlier follow-ups were published in the New England Journal of Medicine and have affected treatment guidelines.

DARS-NIC-656794-C7Q5X.summary: The Institute of Cancer Research is using identifiable cancer registration data on men aged 18 to 79 diagnosed with breast cancer in England and Wales. It uses the data to invite men into a case-control study of the genetic, environmental and behavioural causes of male breast cancer. The aim is better evidence on risk for patients, families and doctors. The study has reported findings, including links with obesity, infertility and genetic risk, which help doctors identify high-risk men.

DARS-NIC-656800-V6B5C.summary: Cancer Research UK, a charity, is using national cancer registration, hospital admission, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy data about people with non-small cell lung cancer. It is evaluating which patient, tumour and provider factors affect access to treatment, and whether access varies between NHS trusts, including chemoradiotherapy and targeted therapies. The main intended benefit is to help those delivering lung cancer services reduce unwarranted variation and improve equitable access to treatment.

DARS-NIC-656801-R9F6Z.summary: University College London (UCL) is using record-level hospital, emergency care and cancer registry data linked to about 10,500 participants in the STAMPEDE prostate cancer trial. It is comparing this data with the information the trial collects itself, covering survival, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, second-line treatment and toxicities. The aim is to show whether routine healthcare data could make trials more efficient. Reported results include a published finding that radiotherapy reduced the risk of urinary tract obstruction, and a published finding that zoledronic acid reduced the risk of fractures.

DARS-NIC-656805-R5Z2Y.summary: Cancer Research UK, a charity, is using pseudonymised National Disease Registration Service data on women diagnosed with ovarian cancer in 2015 and 2016, linked to hospital admissions and systemic anti-cancer therapy records. It is studying how access to ovarian cancer treatment varies across England, and how far patient characteristics and healthcare system factors explain this. The aim is to give evidence that could help reduce variation in care.

DARS-NIC-656806-N9V7N.summary: University College London is using pseudonymised NHS cancer registration, hospital, diagnostic imaging, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy data for people in the Add-Aspirin cancer trial. It will compare this routine data with the trial's own follow-up to see whether it can reliably record outcomes such as survival and cancer recurrence. The aim is to make cancer trials more efficient and less costly. A 2021 paper already described how to access such data for trials.

DARS-NIC-656811-F7T9C.summary: The Clatterbridge Cancer Centre NHS Foundation Trust is using national cancer registration, treatment, and hospital records for people with blood cancer. It is studying how COVID-19 infection affected them and how the pandemic changed their diagnosis, treatment and outcomes. The main intended benefit is to identify who is most at risk, so patients can be protected and treated more appropriately. So far, the project has secured over £400,000 of research funding and involved patient groups, though no analysis has yet been done.

DARS-NIC-656813-F4H5W.summary: University College London (UCL), working with GRAIL, LLC, is using record-level cancer registration, hospital, emergency care, radiotherapy, systemic anti-cancer therapy and related data on people in the SUMMIT study. They are using it to see which cancers participants develop and to assess low-dose CT lung cancer screening and the GRAIL multi-cancer blood test. The main intended benefit is stronger evidence for a national lung cancer screening programme and earlier cancer detection.

DARS-NIC-656815-R5X0N.summary: The London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine is using linked NHS cancer data, covering registrations, waiting times, hospital records, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy. It is studying where patients choose to have specialist cancer treatment and how centralising services affects travel, fairness of access and outcomes. The aim is to give evidence to guide how cancer services are designed. Reported benefits include centralisation models being adopted by NHS England and analysis supporting management of the cancer backlog.

DARS-NIC-656816-Z3N6R.summary: The University of Oxford is using linked National Disease Registration Service data on cancer registrations, hospital care, imaging, radiotherapy and chemotherapy for women with invasive breast cancer. It is checking how accurately an algorithm using routine data identifies breast cancer recurrence, compared with the AZURE trial's recurrence records. The aim is reliable recurrence information to support treatment comparisons and patient prognosis. A peer-reviewed paper on the algorithm was published in BJC Reports in 2025.

DARS-NIC-656818-N1B5Q.summary: The University of Oxford is using NHS England cancer registration, treatment, hospital and radiotherapy data on women diagnosed with early breast cancer. It aims to describe survival, second cancers and other diseases, and to build predictions of the benefits and risks of treatment options. The main intended benefit is that patients and clinicians can make better-informed treatment decisions. Earlier work has already been cited in major breast cancer guidelines, including those from NICE, and used in clinician training.

DARS-NIC-656823-G0Q2C.summary: The University of Leeds is using cancer registration, hospital admissions and systemic anti-cancer therapy data for patients in England who have cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), a liver cancer. It is studying how patients' characteristics and where they live affect which treatment they receive, how long they survive and how their liver disease progresses. The team hopes this will reveal variations in clinical practice and help improve future resource allocation and outcomes.

DARS-NIC-656824-R8K0V.summary: Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust, working with The Christie NHS Foundation Trust, is using identifiable cancer registration, hospital admission, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy data for lung cancer patients treated with curative-intent radiotherapy. They are studying how radiotherapy dose to the heart relates to survival and cardiac death, so that sensitive areas can be given dose limits and side effects reduced. A benefit already reported is that the work informed a dose limit to the base of the heart at The Christie, now being monitored by the RAPID-RT study, and results were presented at ESTRO conferences.

DARS-NIC-656825-X7T4K.summary: University College London (UCL) is using NDRS cancer registration data, covering cancer diagnoses and mortality, for the Advancing Survivorship after Cancer: Outcomes Trial. The trial tests a booklet and health professional feedback aimed at helping cancer survivors improve their health behaviours. The data will help assess whether the intervention improves cancer outcomes and survival, so it could become part of standard NHS care. Earlier data was used to classify participants by diagnosis for analyses in papers due for submission.

DARS-NIC-656826-M3Y6C.summary: Cancer Research UK, a charity, is using pseudonymised, aggregated NDRS Cancer Registrations data on cancer incidence in England, covering 1999 to 2022. It will produce statistics and trends on cancer incidence by factors such as sex, age and stage of diagnosis, answer public queries, and estimate cancers linked to risk factors. These are published on its website and in public reports. The main intended benefit is up-to-date evidence on the state of cancer in the UK for policy-makers, clinicians and patients.

DARS-NIC-656827-P2X2W.summary: The University of Liverpool is using national cancer registration and lung cancer audit data for the UK Lung cancer Screening (UKLS) trial. It will check long-term outcomes for participants and non-participants, and test whether predicted lung cancer risk matches actual cases. The findings are expected to support evidence-based decisions on care. The university has already published papers in Thorax and The Lancet Regional Health - Europe, including an updated risk model and trial results on lung cancer mortality.

DARS-NIC-656830-C3F5S.summary: The University of Leeds is using pseudonymised cancer registration and systemic anti-cancer therapy (chemotherapy) data on people diagnosed with cancer aged 12 to 29. The research looks at whether the dose and intensity of chemotherapy affect one-year and three-year survival, and what makes it harder for patients to receive the ideal dose. The aim is to guide changes in how these patients are treated and to improve outcomes.

DARS-NIC-656832-M8F7G.summary: The University of Nottingham is using national cancer registration data from the National Disease Registration Service (NDRS). The aim is to find out how much healthy tissue should be removed around a breast tumour known as ductal carcinoma in-situ (DCIS) during breast conserving surgery. They will compare the measured margin width with outcomes such as cancer recurrence and survival, with the aim of establishing the optimum margin width.

DARS-NIC-656834-N7Z3Q.summary: Barts Health NHS Trust is using pseudonymised hospital, cancer registration, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy records for people treated for retinoblastoma, a childhood eye cancer, or who carry an RB1 gene mutation. The study looks at whether the type of gene mutation, and the treatment given, affects the risk of developing a second tumour elsewhere in the body later in life. The main intended benefit is closer monitoring of higher-risk patients, which could lead to earlier diagnosis and treatment.

DARS-NIC-656836-T2J0T.summary: Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust holds pseudonymised cancer registration, hospital, cancer waiting times and radiotherapy records from a completed breast cancer clinical trial (the BEA trial). It keeps them securely so the trial analysis can be reconstructed or checked if challenged. The original analysis looked at how socioeconomic status, obesity and diabetes relate to breast cancer recurrence and death, aiming to improve survival and reduce unwarranted variations in care. A draft journal article has been submitted but is not yet published.

DARS-NIC-656837-J7G8S.summary: Erasmus University Medical Centre is using identifiable NHS England cancer registration data on people in England diagnosed with cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (a skin cancer) in 2013 to 2015. It is using the data to build and validate a model that predicts the risk of the cancer spreading, and to compare it with current staging systems. The aim is to help clinicians decide on follow-up care. A prediction model has already been developed, published and made available as an online app, and it performed better than current staging systems.

DARS-NIC-656838-J7H7S.summary: Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust is using pseudonymised cancer registration, hospital, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and patient experience data on adults in England with brain tumours. The project aims to describe patterns of care, outcomes and costs, and to assess how care varies and how this relates to outcomes and costs. It also compares the effect of tumour biology with that of treatment. The study team has published several abstracts and articles on topics including glioblastoma costs and end-of-life care.

DARS-NIC-656839-K5V9L.summary: Queen Mary University of London uses pseudonymised cancer registration, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy data, linked to GP and hospital records in the QResearch database. It supports medical research into causes of disease, treatments and outcomes, including COVID-19 risk prediction, and allows approved UK universities to use the data. The aim is research that benefits patients and the NHS. Reported benefits include the QCancer and QCOVID risk tools, used in clinical practice.

DARS-NIC-656841-D0P8Y.summary: The University of Oxford is using pseudonymised cancer registration, hospital, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and waiting-time data on people diagnosed with primary central nervous system (CNS) tumours. It is studying how common these tumours are, survival, treatments and later health events, with the aim of informing guidelines and care. A paper on incidence trends has been published in Neuro-Oncology, and the work led to the Brain Tumour Data Improvement Initiative.

DARS-NIC-656842-S5V7V.summary: NHS England, with the Healthcare Quality Improvement Partnership (HQIP) and the Royal College of Surgeons' Clinical Effectiveness Unit, uses national cancer registration, treatment, hospital and patient survey data. It uses this data to run the audits of bowel cancer and oesophago-gastric cancer care in England and Wales. The aim is to help services compare themselves, share good practice and improve patient care. Reported results include annual reports with recommendations, and improvements such as more patients with oesophageal high-grade dysplasia being discussed by specialist teams.

DARS-NIC-656843-D8M4Z.summary: University Hospitals Plymouth NHS Trust is using pseudonymised national cancer registration, hospital outpatient, treatment, audit and patient-survey data on people diagnosed with colorectal cancer in England between 2000 and 2014. It is studying the demographics and long-term survival of young patients (aged 40 and under) and comparing them with older patients. The results may help inform screening, public awareness and management of young colorectal cancer patients. Early analysis found regional differences in patient age, deprivation, diagnosis and five-year survival, with findings due for publication.

DARS-NIC-656845-G9J9W.summary: Southampton City Council's Public Health team is using pseudonymised NDRS Cancer Registrations data on cancers diagnosed in Southampton residents and in patients registered with Southampton GP practices. It is being used to audit cancer health inequalities, including by area deprivation and Primary Care Network, to inform local needs assessments, service planning and targeted prevention. The aim is earlier diagnosis. Earlier analysis was used in GP packs and by NHS colleagues in local planning, and the latest data produced a public cancer web page and dashboard.

DARS-NIC-656847-K4L8H.summary: The University of Newcastle upon Tyne is using linked national cancer registration, hospital, treatment, lung cancer audit and molecular test data. It is studying whether access to targeted therapies and immunotherapies differs by factors such as deprivation, and how survival varies. The aim is to inform policy and services so that treatment access is fairer. A published 2023 paper found that non-small cell lung cancer patients in the most deprived areas were 55% less likely to receive these treatments.

DARS-NIC-656848-T9J1Q.summary: The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) runs the Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD), which links GP records to National Disease Registration Service cancer registration data. Approved researchers use the linked, pseudonymised data for observational health research, aiming to improve clinical care, public health policy and regulatory decisions. Published studies have already shown higher flu risks in cancer survivors, which supported vaccination priority guidance.

DARS-NIC-656849-P9M6C.summary: The University of Oxford is using pseudonymised cancer registry, hospital, imaging, radiotherapy and chemotherapy records for people in England diagnosed with lymphoma between 1997 and 2020. It is studying how radiotherapy use varies, how to predict lymphoma recurrence, and long-term effects such as heart disease and second cancers. The aim is to improve understanding of the best management of lymphoma subtypes. Research from this study has already been cited in clinical guidelines and has helped shape clinical trials.

DARS-NIC-656850-Y1V4Q.summary: Leiden University, an academic organisation, is using national cancer registration data, linked hospital records, radiotherapy data and systemic anti-cancer therapy data. It is comparing treatment and survival for patients with gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GIST) across European countries in the EURECCA consortium. The stated aim is to improve understanding of the epidemiology and treatment of GIST in Europe.

DARS-NIC-656851-D6M5H.summary: The Healthcare Quality Improvement Partnership (HQIP), with NHS England, uses pseudonymised cancer registration, hospital, radiotherapy and chemotherapy data on men in England diagnosed with prostate cancer. The Royal College of Surgeons of England runs the National Prostate Cancer Audit, which assesses care and outcomes and compares NHS providers. The aim is to show where care is good and where it can improve. So far, the audit reports fewer under-treated and over-treated patients, and has held two quality improvement workshops.

DARS-NIC-656854-T9G6P.summary: The University of Manchester is using national cancer registration, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy data. It is working out how many patients were cured by radical treatment, meaning no death or further treatment within five years. It then looks at how much each treatment type contributes, and at differences by cancer site, deprivation, ethnic group and age. The expected benefit is scientific publications and conference abstracts. Abstracts have already been presented at scientific conferences.

DARS-NIC-656857-F4D9R.summary: The University of Cambridge is using identifiable cancer registration, outpatient, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy data for people diagnosed with breast, endometrial or ovarian cancer. The SEARCH study looks at how inherited genetic variation affects cancer risk, tumour subtypes, treatment response and survival. Results are intended for peer-reviewed publications. The study's results have already contributed to CanRisk, a cancer risk prediction tool, and PREDICT breast, a prognosis tool used by healthcare professionals.

DARS-NIC-656858-Y9D0P.summary: The University of Leeds is using linked cancer registration, hospital admission, outpatient, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy data. It links these to questionnaire responses from consenting bladder cancer patients in Yorkshire, Humber, South Tees and North Derbyshire. The aim is to describe patients' health-related quality of life, understand variation in outcomes and identify unmet needs, to help improve services. Published papers so far include studies on quality of life after treatment and on sexual function after diagnosis.

DARS-NIC-656860-Q5Q9Q.summary: Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust, with King's College London, is using identifiable cancer registration, hospital, radiotherapy and chemotherapy data on women with lobular or ductal in situ breast cancer who joined the GLACIER and ICICLE studies. They are following up survival and disease progression to see whether genes and tumour markers affect outcomes. The aim is to predict who is likely to develop invasive disease, so treatment can be targeted. The original studies found new links between genetic variations and further breast disease.

DARS-NIC-656861-S5H3R.summary: The London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine is using NDRS cancer registration data for people diagnosed with cancer in England and Wales between 1971 and 2018. It will update the cancer survival index, a single-number summary of survival for all cancers combined up to 10 years after diagnosis. The work is commissioned by Cancer Research UK, which is a joint data controller. The index offers a simple measure for comparing survival over a very long period.

DARS-NIC-656862-L4M7T.summary: The University of Sheffield is using National Disease Registration Service cancer registry data, linked to hospital, radiotherapy and chemotherapy records, for pancreatic cancer research. It will replicate earlier clinical trials with this data and compare the results, to test whether registry data can reliably show how well different cancer treatments work. The aim is better-informed healthcare decisions. So far, the work has produced the first Target Trial replication studies using NHS cancer registry data, and the analyses are complete.

DARS-NIC-656863-R0V6Q.summary: University College London (UCL) is using pseudonymised National Disease Registration Service cancer registration data and National Cancer Diagnosis Audit data for patients diagnosed with cancer in 2014 and 2018. The research looks at how often GPs use tests such as blood tests, endoscopy and imaging before a cancer diagnosis, and how this relates to the time taken to diagnose. It aims to identify opportunities for earlier diagnosis. So far, the findings have identified areas for quality improvement in managing and referring suspected cancer.

DARS-NIC-656866-V3H6X.summary: Health IQ Ltd, a commercial organisation, holds cancer registration, hospital, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy data for men in England with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. It uses them to describe patients' characteristics, treatments, survival and NHS resource use, helping policymakers make informed decisions about care. Results have already been included in a NICE submission on Pluvicto and presented to clinical experts.

DARS-NIC-656867-F3Q3L.summary: Birmingham Women's and Children's NHS Foundation Trust is using congenital anomalies data from the National Disease Registration Service. It is using it for research with the British Paediatric Surveillance Unit to count new cases of congenital ichthyosis in newborn babies in the UK and Ireland, and to study how these babies are managed and how they fare in their first year. The main intended benefit is accurate information to improve care, reduce variation in practice and help avoid deaths.

DARS-NIC-656870-H0K0G.summary: The University of Warwick is using pseudonymised cancer registration, hospital admission, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy data on women invited to breast screening in England. It is studying how screening age, interval and recall threshold affect benefits and harms such as false positive recalls, overdiagnosis and mortality. The aim is to inform the UK National Screening Committee and revisions to breast screening quality assurance guidelines. So far, a paper on the dataset's quality has been published and initial results have been presented to the Breast screening programme board.

DARS-NIC-656873-Q2C7L.summary: The University of Bristol is using pseudonymised national cancer, hospital, diagnostic imaging, radiotherapy and chemotherapy data. It is studying whether people with brain (intracranial) tumours have been diagnosed earlier and more often by hospital eye services since the 2016 Honey Rose court case, and how diagnosis time and route affect survival. The aim is to help design better referral pathways for suspected papilloedema. The results so far have supported two successful National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) grant applications for guidelines and training.

DARS-NIC-656874-T3L9D.summary: University College London (UCL), an academic institution, is using pseudonymised cancer registration data, linked to hospital records, for people diagnosed with cancer who later developed cardiovascular disease. The research examines how well ethnicity is recorded in health data and how often cancer and cardiovascular disease occur together in different ethnic groups. It aims to inform better treatment, prevention and health service planning. A review of COVID-19's impact on multimorbid ethnic minority groups has been published in JACC CardioOncology.

DARS-NIC-656876-L4B0V.summary: University College London (UCL) is using pseudonymised national cancer registration data, including rapid registrations, for adults diagnosed with ten cancers such as lung, breast and bowel cancer. It is modelling how delays to screening, diagnosis and treatment during COVID affect cancer stage at diagnosis, survival and demand for services. The aim is to inform policy and clinical decisions, such as waiting targets, to improve cancer care.

DARS-NIC-656877-H3Z0P.summary: Hampshire Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust is using pseudonymised cancer registration, hospital, imaging, radiotherapy and chemotherapy data on people with neuroendocrine neoplasia, a type of cancer. It is studying how common the cancer is, how people are diagnosed, how long they survive and what their care costs, to inform policy and resource planning. The work has already led to published papers on incidence and survival in England, including sex differences in survival.

DARS-NIC-656879-L3Y5Z.summary: Evidera Ltd, a research company, is using pseudonymised hospital records, cancer registrations and systemic anti-cancer therapy data for adults in England diagnosed with kidney cancer between 2014 and 2018. It is studying treatment patterns and survival in renal cell carcinoma, and how they vary by factors such as stage at diagnosis. The aim is to help healthcare professionals better understand these patients and treatments. Results have already been presented as two conference posters in 2023.

DARS-NIC-656880-K7V7P.summary: Health IQ Ltd, a commercial organisation working for Novartis, is using pseudonymised, non-identifying national cancer registration, treatment, radiotherapy, imaging and hospital records. It is studying the treatment pathway of patients with hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer in England, including differences in access to treatment. The results are intended to support a NICE submission and a journal paper, so that policy decisions are better informed. So far, the results are guiding a future, more specific research project.

DARS-NIC-656881-X0G0X.summary: Norfolk and Norwich University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust is using national data on people in England diagnosed with merkel cell carcinoma, a type of skin cancer, between 2004 and 2018. It is examining how many people are diagnosed each year and how this varies by factors such as age, gender, ethnicity and region. It is also looking at tumour location, stage at diagnosis, treatment and survival. The reported benefit is a better understanding of the disease's incidence, trends, risk factors and mortality.

DARS-NIC-656883-P3K5F.summary: Sandwell and West Birmingham Hospitals NHS Trust is using pseudonymised cancer registration, hospital and systemic anti-cancer therapy data on people diagnosed with oesophageal and stomach cancer. It is studying how well upper gastrointestinal endoscopy detects cancer and which hospital practices reduce the risk of missing it, with the aim of guiding quality improvement. Findings have already been presented at national and international conferences, won a British Society of Gastroenterology award, and appeared in a Gut abstract.

DARS-NIC-656884-R1N3C.summary: The University of Hull is using national cancer registration, cancer pathway, diagnostic imaging and linked hospital admitted patient care data. A single named researcher is studying whether people from different socioeconomic groups differ in how quickly they are diagnosed and treated for colon and ovarian cancer, and in the treatment they receive. The findings are expected to support decisions by policy-makers, clinicians and patients about cancer care. The team has published a paper on inequalities in ovarian cancer diagnosis and treatment in England.

DARS-NIC-656885-M7T5X.summary: The University of Oxford is using pseudonymised NHS England cancer registration, treatment, hospital and patient experience data on everyone diagnosed with bowel and anal cancer since 1997. It is building the CORECT-R research database, which approved researchers can use to study care and outcomes, with the aim of improving bowel cancer care. One published study on post-colonoscopy bowel cancer rates helped providers improve their practice and informed a national audit.

DARS-NIC-656886-D8H1H.summary: Adelphi Group Limited, a consultancy working for Merck Sharp & Dohme (UK) Limited, is using pseudonymised national cancer registration, treatment, radiotherapy and hospital records for adults in England newly diagnosed with locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. It is describing patient characteristics, treatments, outcomes, and healthcare use and costs. The aim is to inform health and social care planning and show where treatment could improve. Results have been presented as a poster at ESMO 2022 and an ASCO 2023 abstract.

DARS-NIC-656887-Q7M1C.summary: Adelphi Group Limited, a consultancy working with Merck Sharp & Dohme (UK) Limited, is using cancer registration, treatment, radiotherapy and hospital records for people in England with locally advanced triple negative breast cancer. They are describing patient characteristics, treatments, outcomes, and healthcare use and costs, to show where treatment could be improved. Results have already been published as an online abstract for the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) 2023 conference.

DARS-NIC-656890-V4L0D.summary: Genomics England, a research organisation, uses NHS England cancer data, including cancer registrations, treatment, radiotherapy, scan and patient survey records. The data is linked to genomic and health data in its National Genomic Research Library for the 100,000 Genomes Project and NHS Genomic Medicine Service cohorts. Researchers use it to study disease, with the aim of better diagnosis and new or more effective treatments. Reported benefits include the genomic database and support for setting up the NHS Genomic Medicine Service.

DARS-NIC-657032-T7Z5C.summary: The University of Oxford, working with King's College London, is using NHS England hospital records (admitted patient care, outpatient and emergency care) and civil registration death records for people with motor neuron disease (MND) in England. It links them to the MND Register's clinical data to estimate how many people have MND, study how the disease progresses and the care people need, and build a mathematical model of MND. The main intended benefit is better evidence for care planning and treatment decisions.

DARS-NIC-657422-S1K1C.summary: The University of York is using linked hospital records (emergency care, admitted patient and outpatient data) for 180 children who are fed through a gastrostomy tube and who joined the "Your Tube" study. It will compare healthcare use and gastrostomy complications between children given formula feeds and those given home-blended food. The aim is to give an evidence base for national clinical guidelines and for parents' and clinicians' decisions.

DARS-NIC-658395-F0F9N.summary: The University of Essex is using school-level results from the National Child Measurement Programme, with a local authority identifier added. It is studying whether universal free school meal schemes run by local authorities in England affect children's bodyweight, including at age 11. The main intended benefit is evidence on whether these schemes reduce childhood overweight and obesity, to inform decisions on funding them.

DARS-NIC-658720-R3V5Z.summary: The University of Warwick is using identifiable NHS England hospital, cancer registration and death records for women aged 50 or over who have had breast cancer surgery. The records support the Mammo-50 trial and a linked observational study. They compare annual mammograms with less frequent ones, looking at survival, recurrence and hospital costs. The aim is to show whether less frequent mammograms are safe and cost-effective, which could inform national guidelines.

DARS-NIC-659282-H1F7C.summary: The Royal Marsden NHS Foundation Trust is using death records, hospital records and national cancer registry data on women treated for Hodgkin Lymphoma at young ages. It is studying their long-term risks of second cancers, other illnesses and death, so patients and clinicians can understand personal risk when choosing treatment and planning follow-up. The text reports that early results helped establish a national high-risk breast screening programme for these women.

DARS-NIC-659283-N1S1H.summary: The London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine's Cancer Survival Group is using cancer registration, pathway, molecular and systemic anti-cancer therapy data for England. It uses them in CONCORD-4, a programme that compares cancer survival trends between countries. The intended benefit is evidence for cancer control policy and for judging health systems. Results from earlier CONCORD cycles have already been used in OECD Health at a Glance publications, WHO reports and EU Country Health Profiles.

DARS-NIC-659284-W0T0H.summary: The University of Cambridge is using identifiable NHS England cancer registration, death, hospital admission, radiotherapy and chemotherapy data for people with oesophageal and junction cancer who consented to the OCCAMS study. It uses the data to identify clinical, demographic and molecular factors affecting how the cancer develops and progresses. The aim is to better tailor treatment plans. The study has produced a revised lymph node classification giving improved prognostic information, and publications showing that circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) levels after surgery can predict relapse.

DARS-NIC-659285-B3X8G.summary: The University of Newcastle upon Tyne is using pseudonymised National Disease Registration Service (NDRS) cancer registration data on head and neck cancers diagnosed in England between 2006 and 2014. It is studying the routes patients take to diagnosis and how these differ by socio-demographic factors and survival, aiming to show where inequalities exist. A published paper found that older age, deprivation and non-white ethnicity increased the likelihood of emergency diagnosis, and the team has secured further research funding.

DARS-NIC-659293-T1G7M.summary: South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust is using pseudonymised cancer registration, hospital, diagnostic imaging and systemic anti-cancer therapy data for people in Lambeth, Southwark, Lewisham and Croydon. It is studying whether people with mental disorders differ from others in cancer incidence, stage at diagnosis, treatment and survival. The aim is to identify inequalities in care so healthcare pathways can be improved. One study has so far compared cancer incidence with expected rates and confirmed earlier findings of lower-than-expected risk.

DARS-NIC-659581-D4B1S.summary: The University of Cambridge is using hospital records for children who took part in the Healthy Start, Happy Start study: Hospital Episode Statistics (admitted patient care, accident and emergency, outpatients) and the Emergency Care Data Set. They will compare NHS service use, and so costs, between families who received a brief parenting programme and those who did not. The aim is to assess the programme's long-term cost-effectiveness for young children at risk of challenging behaviour.

DARS-NIC-66034-M7B8W.summary: RAND Europe Community Interest Company, a research organisation, is using hospital A&E, mental health and talking therapies data to evaluate England's national Liaison and Diversion services, which support people with mental health, substance misuse or learning needs in the criminal justice system. It is examining whether the services change people's use of health services, to help NHS England decide how to commission them. Progress reports and draft findings have been presented to the Department of Health and Social Care and NHS England.

DARS-NIC-660630-L4H3T.summary: Digital Health and Care Wales uses identifiable hospital activity data (Secondary Uses Service data for commissioners) and National Diabetes Audit data about Welsh residents, and people registered with Welsh GP practices, who are treated in England. It uses them for direct care, service planning and commissioning, policy development, public health monitoring and service improvement. The main intended benefit is better management of patient pathways across the Wales-England boundary. The register lists improved patient care and joined-up health care as benefits achieved so far, without naming specific examples.

DARS-NIC-661406-H4V1B.summary: University College London Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust is using hospital, emergency care, outpatient, community mental health and death registration records for children and young people aged 5 to 18 in England. It will describe trends in mental health admissions, A&E attendances and outpatient care, and the financial cost of admissions to paediatric wards. The main intended benefit is better care for children and young people admitted in a mental health crisis.

DARS-NIC-661733-V0T9G.summary: The University of Leeds is using pseudonymised National Disease Registration Service cancer registration data and survey responses from about 34,000 people diagnosed with colorectal cancer who completed a quality of life survey. Two PhD students will test whether patients' own survey answers improve machine learning predictions of cancer survival beyond routine healthcare data. The findings are expected to help inform care, treatment and policy decisions for cancer patients.

DARS-NIC-661736-Y2Q9R.summary: Grail Bio UK Ltd, working with the University of Oxford, is using identifiable contact details from the Personal Demographics Service for fewer than 6,240 adults who joined the SYMPLIFY cancer test trial. The data is used for a mailout asking participants to agree to a further year of medical record follow-up, with a chance to opt out. The aim is to add evidence to inform care and treatment decisions for people affected by cancer. An earlier mailout reportedly enabled GRAIL LLC to complete its analysis of the test.

DARS-NIC-661742-Y2K8L.summary: The University of Leicester is using pseudonymised hospital, mental health, community services, diabetes audit and death registration data for people aged 65 and over in England. The research looks at how many physical health conditions older people receiving mental health care have, compared with those who do not, and how these relate to outcomes. It aims to inform recommendations for improving physical health care for people with complex physical and mental health needs.

DARS-NIC-661854-W9V1H.summary: The University of Sheffield is using pseudonymised national cancer registry data linked to hospital, radiotherapy, cancer waiting times and systemic anti-cancer therapy records for adults with prostate or kidney cancer. It is testing whether this real-world data can reliably compare the effectiveness of treatments given in sequence, by replicating the results of two clinical trials. The main intended benefit is evidence on whether these data can support NHS treatment decisions where trial data are lacking.

DARS-NIC-662234-T6B7J.summary: The University of Leicester is using record-level pseudonymised NHS England cancer registration data, plus data on the quality of life of colorectal cancer survivors in England. It is developing new statistical methods to show how a cancer diagnosis affects survival and quality of life, and how interventions or the COVID-19 pandemic affect outcomes. The main intended benefit is better methods for future cancer survival research. So far, the team has extended methods for imputing missing cancer stage, which others will now use.

DARS-NIC-662451-S5L8J.summary: Milton Keynes University Hospital NHS Foundation Trust is using pseudonymised hospital admission records and civil death registrations for 2,667 patients who had a stress echocardiogram for chest pain. It will follow their outcomes for up to 15 years and use machine learning to build a model predicting major cardiovascular events. The intended benefit is more accurate diagnosis, potentially reducing the need for invasive diagnostic procedures and freeing NHS resources.

DARS-NIC-662465-L3R5W.summary: Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust is using identifiable hospital admission records and death registration data for a clinical trial of people receiving dialysis for end-stage kidney disease. The trial tests whether lowering blood phosphate levels towards the normal level reduces deaths and major heart and circulation events, compared with a more relaxed target. The findings are intended to inform clinical guidelines, including those from NICE.

DARS-NIC-663093-K1B0K.summary: Ipsos (Market Research) Ltd, working for the Department of Health and Social Care, uses NHS England maternity and demographic data to select mothers of newborn babies in England and send them the Infant Feeding Survey. The survey aims to produce national estimates of breastfeeding and other infant feeding practices. The main intended benefit is an up-to-date evidence base to help government shape policy, guidance and support for infant feeding.

DARS-NIC-663381-C9W8N.summary: The London Borough of Bexley is using Hospital Episode Statistics and Emergency Care Data Set records, covering hospital admissions, outpatients, critical care and A&E. It uses them for its public health work, including needs assessments, health and wellbeing strategies, commissioning and advice to NHS commissioners. The aim is locally focused analysis of health inequalities. In frailty profiling, the data helped build a business case with NHS and Adult Social Care partners to reconfigure frailty services in the borough.

DARS-NIC-663539-G7F9X.summary: The Royal College of Surgeons of England's Clinical Effectiveness Unit is using national cancer registration, hospital, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy data to run the National Lung Cancer Audit. The audit evaluates the quality of NHS lung cancer care in England and Wales against standards, and highlights unexplained variation between hospitals. Its main intended benefit is helping NHS services benchmark themselves and improve care. Reports have already shown rising curative treatment rates and led to quarterly reporting from 2023.

DARS-NIC-664431-F3G8W.summary: The University of Birmingham is using hospital, outpatient, imaging, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and death records for 143 patients in the BladderPath bladder cancer trial. It will follow them for up to 24 months to see whether their disease progressed and when. The trial tests whether an MRI scan instead of a surgical procedure (TURBT) avoids unnecessary surgery and speeds up treatment for muscle invasive bladder cancer.

DARS-NIC-664530-K6Q5H.summary: Imperial College London, an academic institution, is using pseudonymised NDRS Cancer Registration data on women in England diagnosed with anal and genital cancer or high-grade precancerous lesions (HSIL). The research, part of a PhD thesis, aims to establish how many women with anal cancer or HSIL have also had a genital diagnosis, and which sociodemographic factors affect risk. The intended benefit is to identify who would gain from closer anogenital surveillance, supporting earlier diagnosis and guidelines for early detection.

DARS-NIC-666525-M8L1F.summary: The University of Leeds is using hospital, emergency care, mental health, medicines and death registration data to study people who attend emergency departments frequently. It aims to understand their patterns of use and costs, and how well current services work. The main intended benefit is evidence to help plan better services for these patients. Findings have already been shared with NHS service teams and presented to the Department of Health and Social Care.

DARS-NIC-667040-B5T1X.summary: The Centre for Health Economics at the University of York uses NHS England hospital, mental health, community, cancer, death registration and medicines data. It uses them for research on health economics, including evaluating health interventions, policy impacts, inequalities and healthcare performance. The aim is to give policymakers evidence on getting the best value from limited NHS resources. Reported benefits include evidence for policymakers on mental health crisis care services, and findings on how new heart attack care technologies affect costs and survival.

DARS-NIC-667506-N6Q9G.summary: The London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine is using pseudonymised hospital, emergency care and death registration data on adults with chronic liver disease admitted to hospital as an emergency. The research looks at how treatment and services affect care and outcomes, so that care can be organised and delivered better nationally. A method for identifying first emergency admissions has been published in JHEP Reports, and findings have been presented at a liver conference.

DARS-NIC-667559-J3L9G.summary: The University of Oxford, working with the University of Bristol, is using pseudonymised hospital admission, death registration and patient-reported outcome data for people who had hip, knee, foot or ankle surgery. They are studying how often complications and repeat operations occur, and whether outcomes differ with surgeon and hospital unit volume. The aim is to set benchmarks for monitoring care quality and to help patients and surgeons understand the risks of these procedures.

DARS-NIC-668928-L9N5F.summary: The University of Oxford is using hospital, emergency care, cancer registration and death registration records. It is linking them with lung health check data to develop artificial intelligence tools for diagnosing lung cancer earlier and to improve predictions of patient outcomes. The main intended benefit is more accurate and quicker lung cancer diagnosis, and better selection of people for lung cancer screening.

DARS-NIC-669808-V6T0M.summary: Cardiff University, an academic organisation, is using demographic data to match identifiers so that National Paediatric Diabetes Audit records can be linked with education data in the Office for National Statistics secure research service. The study examines how diabetes-related health and educational outcomes are connected. It aims to give evidence that could shape policy and support for children and students with diabetes. So far, the team has presented findings to clinicians, patients and researchers, and a first paper was accepted by Diabetes Care.

DARS-NIC-669962-W1F6D.summary: Cardiff University, an academic institution, is using National Diabetes Audit data on diabetes diagnosis, blood glucose levels and care processes for people in England and Wales. It is studying how education and diabetes-related health are linked, using linked administrative data. The aim is to build evidence that could inform changes in policy and practice to support children with diabetes. So far, the team has presented findings to clinicians, patients and researchers, and supplied evidence to two policy consultations in Wales and England.

DARS-NIC-670080-S6J0Y.summary: The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), the World Health Organisation's cancer agency, is using pseudonymised cancer registration data from NHS England's National Disease Registration Service. It will study how COVID-19 affected cancer diagnosis, stage, treatment and survival, as part of an international benchmarking partnership. The aim is to help countries plan ways to reduce the pandemic's indirect impact on cancer services and patients.

DARS-NIC-67135-G7D9V.summary: The University of Dundee is using linked hospital admission and death records, with pseudonymised data on trial participants, to find heart attacks, strokes and deaths in the TIME study. The study tests whether taking blood pressure medicines in the morning or the evening better prevents heart attacks and strokes. The main results found no clinically significant difference, and they have been included in international hypertension guidelines.

DARS-NIC-671668-B4T0T.summary: The University of Manchester's rapid evaluation teams (REVAL-GM and Rose-NET) are using NHS England hospital, emergency care, outpatient, community and maternity data. They are using it to evaluate new ways of working in health and care services, chosen by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), by looking at changes in service use before and after each innovation is introduced. The main intended benefit is evidence to help commissioners, policymakers and providers improve services and patient access and outcomes. No specific benefit has yet been reported.

DARS-NIC-671672-G6R6W.summary: The London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine is using pseudonymised, England-wide national cancer registration, treatment, hospital, imaging and patient survey data. It is developing and validating methods to identify when bowel cancer has come back after curative treatment, and testing them on other cancers. The aim is to make recurrence routinely measurable, supporting research, monitoring of care and clinical trials. So far, the work has produced internally validated algorithms for identifying metastatic cancer and recurrence.

DARS-NIC-672111-H3R2T.summary: Imperial College London, an academic organisation, is using identifiable NHS England data on hospital admissions, demographics, mental health services, talking therapies and the National Diabetes Audit. The data covers 9,936 people in the ADDRESS-2 study, who consented to follow-up after a type 1 diabetes diagnosis. The university will study long-term health, including mental health and diabetes complications. The main intended benefit is identifying new risk factors and prevention targets to reduce long-term illness.

DARS-NIC-67398-K2Y3T.summary: Imperial College London is using record-level, pseudonymised hospital data covering inpatient, outpatient and accident and emergency care in England from 2011/12 to 2021/22. It is studying how connected hospital providers are and how fragmented patient care is between them. The aim is to help clinicians and NHS England understand patient transfers and identify hospitals vulnerable to rising demand or cyber-attacks. Published papers have already informed North West London care planning and a Royal College of Surgeons response to COVID-19.

DARS-NIC-674735-Z0H6K.summary: Cardiff University, an academic organisation, is using demographic data from NHS England, with identifiers passed on for linkage in the Office for National Statistics, to study how diabetes-related health and education outcomes are linked in children and young people. The aim is to build evidence that could inform changes to policy and practice, and to help clinicians support them better. So far, the team has presented findings to clinicians, patients and researchers, and a first paper was accepted by the journal Diabetes Care.

DARS-NIC-674822-S2K9T.summary: The University of Oxford, with Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, is using NHS England's DigiTrials Patient List Update Service to check whether very young children in the Children's Surgery Outcome Reporting (CSOR) study have died, and to get current contact addresses. This stops study communications reaching bereaved parents or guardians. The main intended benefit is to keep contact going with parents while avoiding distress. So far, hospitals have used the CSOR data to plan changes, such as a decision-making framework for infants with necrotising enterocolitis at Southampton.

DARS-NIC-674976-S4T1V.summary: University College London researchers are using the Adult Psychiatric Morbidity Survey 2014, a national mental health survey dataset, for a PhD study. They are examining how "complex emotional needs" (also described as personality disorder traits) relate to loneliness, self-harm and suicidal thoughts, and the role of discrimination. The main intended benefit is evidence to help develop interventions that target loneliness.

DARS-NIC-675446-G2S5Q.summary: The University of Hull is using pseudonymised cancer registration, treatment, hospital and patient survey data for adults in Yorkshire and Humberside and the North East. It is studying whether longer travel times and distances to care are linked to differences in cancer stage, treatment and survival, including for people in coastal communities. Findings could guide extra support for patients who travel further. Results have been presented at conferences and used in a PhD thesis, which informed local Cancer Alliance work on where to place mobile lung health checks.

DARS-NIC-67693-R7J5Y.summary: London Borough of Ealing, a local authority, uses civil registration data on births and deaths, plus primary care mortality data, which includes identifiable information. It uses the data to understand local health needs, plan services and protect public health, including through suicide audits and hotspot mapping. The intended benefit is local services better targeted to reduce premature deaths and health inequalities. Birth information has already informed its Joint Strategic Needs Assessment, the Director of Public Health's annual report and commissioning plans.

DARS-NIC-678273-F2S0V.summary: University College London is using national cancer registration, treatment, hospital admission, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and tumour gene data about people with lung cancer. It will build and test several statistical and machine learning models that predict survival and other outcomes, to see which works best. The aim is to support better treatment decisions for people with lung cancer, with clinicians and patients better able to rely on accurate predictions.

DARS-NIC-680303-Y3X4W.summary: The University of Oxford is using identifiable hospital admission, emergency care and death registration records for about 3,000 trial participants aged 75 or over who take blood pressure medicines. It is using them to compare emergency hospital admissions and deaths between people who stop or reduce these medicines and those who continue. The aim is to show the longer-term effects of reducing blood pressure treatment, to inform clinical guidelines for older adults.

DARS-NIC-680546-S0V4K.summary: University College London is using pseudonymised hospital admission, emergency care and civil registration death records for adults in England with stroke or stroke-like symptoms. It is studying how prehospital video triage, used since 2020 in four areas, affects patient transfer, care, outcomes such as length of stay and deaths, and value for money. The main intended benefit is to inform national guidelines and decisions on whether to roll out this triage for stroke patients.

DARS-NIC-680871-G5H4X.summary: The University of Newcastle upon Tyne is using NHS Business Services Authority data on medicines dispensed in primary care, linked to women recruited to the SWEET study. It is testing whether prescription records can measure how well women with early breast cancer take their hormone therapy after treatment. The wider programme aims to support women to keep taking this therapy, which could reduce the chance of breast cancer returning.

DARS-NIC-681645-M2G8X.summary: Swansea University is using pseudonymised hospital admission, accident and emergency, critical care and death registration data from NHS England. It is studying how introducing Emergency Admission Risk Stratification (EARS) tools affected emergency admissions, emergency department attendances, intensive care use, time in hospital, deaths and NHS costs. The intended benefit is evidence to help policy-makers decide on the future use of these tools in primary care.

DARS-NIC-681965-Y4H5P.summary: Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust is using national cancer registry data on people diagnosed with cutaneous melanoma between 1995 and 2018. This includes registrations, hospital records, radiotherapy, systemic anti-cancer therapy and molecular data. The Trust is using it to build and test an online PREDICT Melanoma tool that estimates individual outcomes. It aims to help patients and clinicians make better-informed decisions about investigations and treatment.

DARS-NIC-682048-S9P4H.summary: Certara UK, a commercial company, is using pseudonymised NHS England cancer registration, hospital, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy records. It is studying the healthcare use and costs of graft versus host disease in adults with blood cancers who have had a donor stem cell transplant in England. The aim is to show the unmet need and support better treatment, planning and use of resources.

DARS-NIC-68229-Y5J6V.summary: King's College London, an academic institution, is using Hospital Episode Statistics data on hospital admissions, outpatient visits and A&E attendances. It is using this data in the CODES trial, which tests cognitive behavioural therapy for people with dissociative (non-epileptic) seizures. The data will show whether treatment reduces use of healthcare services. The intended benefit is evidence that could inform NHS care pathways and reduce NHS spending.

DARS-NIC-682461-D0Z7H.summary: Imperial College London, an academic organisation, is using cancer registration data and linked hospital admitted patient and outpatient records. The data covers people with Lynch Syndrome, an inherited condition that raises cancer risk. It is being used in a pilot registry study to understand how these patients are monitored and managed, including how common cancer diagnoses are and the quality of colonoscopy surveillance. The main intended benefit is better evidence to improve care and to support the national Bowel Cancer Screening Programme's management of Lynch Syndrome surveillance.

DARS-NIC-682529-F0V1M.summary: Royal Free London NHS Foundation Trust is using pseudonymised 2018 National Cancer Diagnosis Audit data from London GP practices, linked to National Disease Registration Service cancer registrations. It aims to identify factors linked to late or delayed cancer diagnosis, by demographic group and tumour type, to support planning and earlier diagnosis. Analysis of pancreatic cancer data has already led to a wider age range for direct access abdominal CT scans across London.

DARS-NIC-682532-B4B5L.summary: Hull University Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust is using pseudonymised national cancer registry data on adults diagnosed with melanoma between 2016 and 2022. The study compares how often people with head and neck melanoma are offered sentinel lymph node biopsy, a staging procedure, across England, and what treatment and outcomes follow. It aims to show whether access should be widened. Findings so far show access varies by where people live and by area deprivation, and are being prepared for publication.

DARS-NIC-682551-T8V0S.summary: University of Southampton is using identifiable NHS England cancer registration data for 23,801 consenting patients who went to their GP with lung or colorectal symptoms. The researchers will link the data to patients' symptoms and test samples to build and validate prediction rules for lung and colorectal cancer. The aim is to help GPs quickly sort patients into those who can be reassured and those needing cancer investigations, potentially speeding up diagnosis.

DARS-NIC-682554-L6G6Q.summary: The University of York is using pseudonymised hospital, cancer registration, chemotherapy and radiotherapy records for around 4,000 children, teenagers and young adults who died from cancer in England between 2012 and 2020. The researchers want to find out whether the use of high intensity treatments near the end of life varies with the model of end of life care a treatment centre provides. They hope the findings will inform NICE guidelines and the planning and funding of children's end of life care.

DARS-NIC-682565-F6C6T.summary: Queen Mary University of London is using identifiable NHS England cancer registration data (the NDRS Cancer Consolidated Data Set) for women with gynaecological cancers discussed at specialist team meetings at sites in the UK COVID and Gynaecological Cancer Study. The study will examine how COVID-19 changes to care and treatment delays affected long-term outcomes such as recurrence and survival. The aim is to help policymakers and clinicians plan better care during future health crises.

DARS-NIC-682571-Q6Z6Y.summary: The University of Leeds is using identifiable NHS England cancer registration, hospital admission, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and diagnostic imaging data for about 2,000 consenting bowel cancer patients in Yorkshire and the Humber. It links this data to the patients' questionnaire responses about their quality of life. The aim is to understand differences in outcomes across the region and to feed findings back to hospital teams, so that care and patient outcomes can improve.

DARS-NIC-682583-Z3V2H.summary: Adelphi Real World, a commercial organisation, is using linked NHS England cancer registration, treatment, hospital, A&E, outpatient and diagnostic imaging data for patients with early-stage or locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer. The study will describe patient characteristics, treatment patterns, healthcare use, costs and survival outcomes. It aims to highlight gaps in treatment and inform the use of new treatments, such as immunotherapy, to improve patient outcomes.

DARS-NIC-682587-K5N5K.summary: The UK Health Security Agency is using identifiable cancer registration data from the National Disease Registration Service for a long-term study of 43,690 UK servicemen, some of whom attended atmospheric nuclear weapons tests between 1952 and 1967. The study compares their cancer and mortality rates with those of servicemen who did not attend and with the general population. It aims to give test veterans evidence on whether their health was affected. Four analyses have been published in scientific journals, and the Ministry of Defence uses the evidence when considering matters such as War pensions.

DARS-NIC-682588-Z0V8G.summary: The UK Health Security Agency uses identifiable individual-level NHS England cancer registration data, with linked demographics data, for people who have worked with radiation for participating employers. It uses the data in the long-running National Registry for Radiation Workers study, which examines how long-term occupational radiation exposure affects workers' health, especially cancer and mortality. The main intended benefit is stronger evidence on radiation risks for public health and emergency planning. Scientific papers from earlier analyses have been published open access, with plain-language summaries online.

DARS-NIC-683842-M6S8N.summary: Lane Clark & Peacock LLP, a consultancy, is using NHS hospital inpatient, outpatient and civil death registration data. It is analysing delays in gynaecological care and ethnic inequalities in coronary heart disease treatment for clients including the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists and the British Heart Foundation. The aim is to help decision makers understand health needs and address inequalities. So far, a public online dashboard on gynaecology waiting lists has been built.

DARS-NIC-683852-F5X4W.summary: The London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, working with the University of Bristol, is using hospital admission, outpatient and critical care records linked to death registration data. The study looks at people having surgery for common vascular conditions, comparing urgent with scheduled operations, including before and during COVID-19. The main intended benefit is to show which patient groups should be prioritised for urgent surgery, to inform clinical practice and guidance.

DARS-NIC-684835-V0W0X.summary: The University of Oxford, working with Bangor University, is using pseudonymised hospital admissions, emergency care, critical care and outpatient records for people who took part in the SuMMiT-D trial. The data will be used to cost hospital care and compare the cost-effectiveness of supporting people with type 2 diabetes through brief text messages against usual care. The main intended benefit is to show NHS decision-makers whether this support offers value for money.

DARS-NIC-685917-H4X8G.summary: Imperial College London and NHS Blood and Transplant (NHSBT) are using pseudonymised hospital admission, critical care and COVID-19 treatment records for about 10,000 consenting solid organ transplant recipients. They are studying whether people with COVID-19 antibodies after vaccination are less likely to be hospitalised or die from COVID-19, to help guide advice for specific patient groups. The study's findings have been published in The Lancet, reporting that having antibodies was linked to lower rates of infection and hospitalisation.

DARS-NIC-686058-N9C5V.summary: The London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine is using hospital records (emergency care, admitted patient and outpatient data) for a consenting group of homeless adults in London. It is comparing hospital use between people who had contact with a peer advocate from the Groundswell homeless health peer advocacy programme and people who did not, focusing on attendance at scheduled outpatient appointments. The intended benefit is evidence to guide future peer advocacy services.

DARS-NIC-68697-R6F1T.summary: Dr Foster Limited, now Telstra Health UK, uses pseudonymised hospital, emergency care and death registration data. It uses them to build online benchmarking tools, bespoke analyses and published research that help NHS organisations compare quality, mortality, length of stay and efficiency. The aim is better decisions and, ultimately, better patient care. Reported results include a COVID-19 mortality dashboard, a homelessness report and analysis of admissions during the first pandemic wave, published in the Daily Telegraph.

DARS-NIC-68703-R4Y6C.summary: The University of Oxford is using hospital admissions records (Hospital Episode Statistics) linked to civil registration death data. It is studying knee arthroscopy, knee replacement and foot and ankle surgery, looking at rates of surgery, complications, outcomes and variation across England. The aim is to help reduce unnecessary surgery and standardise treatment choices. Several journal articles have been published, including findings on complication risks and a 2018 guidance on meniscal surgery.

DARS-NIC-687052-V2Q0M.summary: University of Liverpool is using pseudonymised cancer registration, treatment, hospital, and diagnostic imaging data for patients in England who were diagnosed with breast cancer at 16 or over. It is auditing survival, how often cancer spreading to the brain and spinal cord is seen, and how it is diagnosed and treated, to help inform NHS policy and treatment decisions. So far, analysis shows survival has improved over time and differs by breast cancer subtype.

DARS-NIC-687063-J3V2C.summary: The University of Exeter, working with University College London, is using pseudonymised cancer registration and National Cancer Diagnosis Audit data on people diagnosed with cancer in England. It is studying how GPs use tests, such as blood tests and imaging, for patients who later receive a cancer diagnosis, and why use varies between practices. The aim is to identify opportunities for earlier diagnosis. The study has so far identified areas for quality improvement in managing and referring suspected cancer.

DARS-NIC-68740-X7R2N.summary: Barts Health NHS Trust is using hospital admission records and death registration data for 7,045 UK surgical patients who consented to linkage in the International Surgical Outcomes Study. It is studying long-term survival and hospital use after surgery, including how early complications relate to later death. The aim is to inform how surgery is planned and delivered. A published paper has already shown that socioeconomic deprivation is linked to poorer long-term survival.

DARS-NIC-687582-X2P3K.summary: The Department for Business and Trade, through its Office for Product Safety and Standards (OPSS), is using record-level, pseudonymised Emergency Care Data Set (ECDS) data from April 2022 onwards. It will use the data to measure and track injuries from consumer products, spot emerging trends and understand who is affected and how. The main intended benefit is better policy, regulation and targeted communications to help prevent product-related injuries.

DARS-NIC-687619-P7W5V.summary: Middlesbrough Borough Council, a local authority, uses civil registration data on births and deaths, plus primary care mortality data, which includes identifiable details. It uses the data to measure local health needs, plan services and immunisation programmes, protect public health and run suicide audits. Results are published as aggregated statistics. The main intended benefit is local services tailored to areas of greatest need, aiming to reduce mortality and health inequalities.

DARS-NIC-68774-M1W6Q.summary: The University of York is using linked hospital admission records, civil registration death records and National Audit of Cardiac Rehabilitation data. It is studying whether modern cardiac rehabilitation, as delivered in routine practice, reduces deaths, hospital re-admissions and repeat heart attacks over five years, by comparing people who attended with those who did not. The aim is to inform future NHS decisions on whether cardiac rehabilitation should continue to be funded.

DARS-NIC-687867-Y7L9P.summary: NHS Lincolnshire Integrated Care Board is using hospital activity data (SUS for Commissioners), linked to information from wearables, smartphone sensors and online questionnaires completed by consenting participants. It is testing whether this combined data can predict demand for health services and adverse healthcare events. The intended benefit is to help the NHS step in sooner, target vulnerable patients before they need hospital admission, and redesign services.

DARS-NIC-688223-X1W4R.summary: The University of Nottingham, an academic organisation, is using identifiable NHS England cancer registration and death registration records for about 1,500 women in the POSNOC trial. The trial is testing whether adjuvant therapy alone is no worse than adjuvant therapy plus axillary treatment (treatment of the armpit lymph nodes) for women with early-stage breast cancer and one or two affected sentinel nodes. The records will be used to follow recurrence and survival over ten years. The main intended benefit is evidence to guide future breast cancer treatment guidelines.

DARS-NIC-688768-Y9Q9S.summary: The Institute of Cancer Research is using cancer registration, hospital admission, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy data on patients treated with radiotherapy for oropharyngeal cancer in England. It will compare their demographics with those of patients in the TORPEdO proton beam therapy trial, to see whether the trial represented the wider population. The intended benefit is fairer design of future proton beam therapy trials and better-informed commissioning decisions.

DARS-NIC-689512-S9R2Q.summary: Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust is using National Cancer Registration and Analysis Service cancer registration, treatment, hospital care, radiotherapy and chemotherapy data on people with T- and NK-cell lymphomas in England. It is studying how often these rare lymphomas occur, how patients are treated and how long they survive, including differences by deprivation, ethnicity and region. The aim is to support better diagnosis, outcomes and disease management. Two papers have been published, on hepatosplenic and enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma.

DARS-NIC-689987-Z6D2Z.summary: King's College London is using pseudonymised cancer registration data on men aged 65 to 79 in Sheffield, Rotherham and Doncaster who have been diagnosed with bladder cancer. The data will be used to calculate bladder cancer incidence rates and compare them with a consented group of participants in YORKSURe, a feasibility trial of early detection through testing for non-visible blood in urine. The main intended benefit is to show whether a larger trial is viable, which could lead to earlier detection and better survival.

DARS-NIC-690385-R5D4B.summary: Lancaster University, an academic institution, is using hospital, emergency care, mental health service, alcohol dependency and death registration data. The research looks at how often people using mental health services also have an alcohol use disorder, how their treatment pathways differ, and how longer-term outcomes such as mortality compare, with a particular focus on bipolar disorder. The main intended benefit is evidence to help target alcohol screening and referrals and to improve care and access for this group.

DARS-NIC-691697-K9L9B.summary: University College London (UCL) is using NHS England records on deaths, demographics, and hospital, emergency and outpatient care for people who received pituitary-derived human growth hormone between 1959 and 1985. It will build two research databases: one to check whether recipients have higher rates of death or hospital care for neurological conditions such as stroke and dementia, and one listing people who agree to be contacted about future research. The main intended benefit is to confirm whether recipients are at risk of these conditions, so they can be monitored and cared for.

DARS-NIC-692254-N3J5W.summary: University College London (UCL), an academic organisation, is using pseudonymised NHS England hospital, cancer registration and death records for men identified as subfertile through the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority register. It is studying their risks of long-term cancers, other health conditions and early death, compared with men from the general population. The main intended benefit is better evidence on the long-term health needs of subfertile men, to help with early detection and prevention.

DARS-NIC-692602-Q6P4F.summary: Neo Health Hub Limited, a commercial company, uses linked hospital data (Emergency Care Data Set, Hospital Episode Statistics admitted patient care and outpatients) with medicines dispensed in primary care. It builds dashboards, reports and bespoke analyses on prescribing and its links to hospital activity, for NHS bodies and approved others, aiming to improve prescribing and patient safety. NHS medicines optimisation teams already use its free respiratory and insomnia dashboards, and it has produced requested custom analyses.

DARS-NIC-694476-T3R6K.summary: The University of Aberdeen is using hospital admissions and outpatient records for 387 women in England who took part in the HEALTH trial. It is following them for five to eight years to compare two treatments for heavy menstrual bleeding: laparoscopic supracervical hysterectomy and endometrial ablation. The study looks at further treatment, late side effects and cost-effectiveness. It aims to help patients, clinicians and NHS decision-makers choose between the treatments.

DARS-NIC-694500-C0W0K.summary: The Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) is using pseudonymised data from the Surgical Devices and Implants Data Set, including its Pelvic Floor Registry module. It will analyse how many pelvic mesh or tape procedures, and alternatives, were recorded for stress urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse. The aim is to test whether this data can support safety monitoring of pelvic mesh devices. The main intended benefit is better-informed regulatory vigilance and decisions on mesh use.
